ann_84.original: Hypothesis (supported): additive logit backbone, an identity node over the 36 direct input->output edges. Formula: -0.997 voiceMailPlan + 0.811 totalEveMinutes + 0.724 internationalPlan + 0.704 totalDayMinutes + 0.396 numberVmailMessages + 0.262 totalNightCharge - 0.201 totalIntlCalls + 0.119 totalDayCalls + 0.102 accountLength - 0.009 totalEveCalls + 0.007 totalNightCalls + 25 state offsets (|w|<=0.20 per z, largest state:46 -0.20, state:47 +0.17, state:4 +0.13, state:31 +0.11, state:0 -0.11). Evidence: exact closed form; sensitivity equals |weights|. One-hot offsets on train: internationalPlan +2.47 logit (calibrating +2.43), voiceMailPlan -2.26 net of the vmail-messages slope (calibrating -2.31). numberCustomerServiceCalls and totalDayCharge have no direct edges (their effects run through the gates); eve usage enters positively here as eveMinutes and negatively in the csc gate as eveCharge (identical after z-scoring).
ann_84.proposed: A straight-line part in which an international plan raises the predicted chance most.

ann_85.original: Hypothesis (supported): service calls x low total usage. 104 = relu(0.228 + 0.383 CSC - 1.051 dayCharge - 0.995 eveCharge + 0.074 state30 + 0.101 state6), read out 0.911. The unit is on (56% of rows) when calls are many or combined day+evening charge is low. Evidence (train, 4000 rows): mean logit contribution 2.15 (0 calls) to 3.99 (5 calls) in the lowest decile of day+eve charge, 0 above the median for <=3 calls, and still +1.3 at 7+ calls in p50-75. Sensitivity: dayCharge 0.59, eveCharge 0.55, CSC 0.21, states 30/6 0.04-0.06. Part of it cancels the positive linear day/eve slopes for light users. Linearising it alone costs 0.008 train AUC; restoring it alone onto the all-linear model gains 0.037.
ann_85.proposed: Higher daytime and evening charges lower the predicted chance, more so when the evening charge is low and for customers in Connecticut.

ann_86.original: Hypothesis (supported): a service-calls threshold vetoed by high day charge, with a small intl-minutes / state-42 modulation of the veto. 10528 = relu(0.726 + 1.02 state42 - 0.449 intlMinutes) (on for 92% of rows); 2963 = relu(0.527 + 1.022 dayCharge - 0.443 h10528) (the veto, on for 59%); 7506 = relu(-0.681 + 0.84 CSC - 2.757 h2963) fires from 3 calls when day charge is below about its median (10% of rows); read out 1.628 h7506 + 1.609 relu(1.201 h7506 - 0.09). Evidence (train): 0 for 0-2 calls; +0.71 at 3 calls, +3.0 at 4, +5.3 at 5, +7.6 at 6, +9.9 at 7+ when day charge <p25; ~0 above p75. Joint with csc_low_usage_gate the model reproduces the empirical pattern: CSC>=4 with day charge <p25 churns 0.90-1.00 (model 0.75-0.82); CSC>=4 at p50-90 churns 0.19-0.20 (model 0.17-0.21). The state-42 route switches the veto off for state 42 rows (68 rows): +0.94 logit at 3 calls, +3.23 at 4 calls on 8 rows of which 2 churned, a rare-category interaction with no support. Replacing 10528 by its mean changes train AUC by only 0.0007. This child carries the largest nonlinear gain: linearising it alone costs 0.025 AUC; restoring it alone onto the all-linear model gains 0.053.
ann_86.proposed: Customer-service calls raise the predicted chance for the customers this part acts on, more so in Tennessee.

ann_87.original: Hypothesis (supported): high-usage hinge. 6238 = relu(-0.514 + 0.886 dayMinutes - 0.015 state34), read out 2.24. Zero below the median, +0.70 logit at p75-90 and +2.35 above p90, where churn is 0.49 (vs 0.06-0.15 below). Adds to the linear +0.70 dayMinutes slope (dayMinutes == dayCharge after z-scoring, so this and the dayCharge veto read the same quantity). state34's weight is negligible (sensitivity 0.004). Restoring it alone onto the all-linear model gains 0.031 train AUC; linearising it alone costs 0.005.
ann_87.proposed: Daytime minutes raise the predicted chance above about 212 minutes.

ann_88.original: Hypothesis (weakly supported, nearly inert): 11575 = relu(1.064 accountLength - 1.262), read out 0.229: extra slope for the longest-tenure 12% (z>1.19), on top of the direct +0.10 slope. Contribution <=0.15 logit on average in the top decile; churn is not clearly higher there (0.16 vs 0.13). Linearising it changes train AUC by <0.0001: a small fitted bend.
ann_88.proposed: A longer account adds slightly above an account length of about 147.

ann_89.original: Hypothesis (supported, mostly linear): 29980 = relu(1.042 intlMinutes + 0.39), read out 0.402. Zero for the lowest ~quarter of intl minutes, then linear: +0.28 at p50-75, +0.87 above p90 (churn 0.22 vs 0.11-0.14). It replaces a direct intl-minutes edge (there is none); linear R2 0.81, linearising costs 0.0006 AUC.
ann_89.proposed: International minutes add slightly above about 9 minutes.

ann_90.original: Hypothesis (supported): effectively linear. 25620 = relu(0.867 numberVmailMessages - 0.104), read out 0.048: on for the 26% of rows with voicemail messages, <=0.13 logit; linear R2 0.98. Together with the direct +0.396 slope and voiceMailPlan -0.997 it makes voicemail users lower-risk with a small upward slope in message count.

ann_91.original: Hypothesis (supported): exact single-state offsets. Each unit depends only on mutually exclusive one-hots, so it is exactly affine in them (linear R2 1.0). 597 = relu(0.564 - 0.131 state48) switches off for state 48 (+0.25, net state48 -0.35); 1084 = relu(0.786 state40 + 0.044) +0.05 for state 40; 11236 = relu(0.747 state24 + 2.23) is always on, giving state 24 a -1.60 logit offset (80 rows, 9 churners; raw empirical log-odds -0.27, calibrating offset given the other features -0.55: the network over-shoots by ~1 logit, an in-sample ranking fit to a rare category); 9802 = relu(1.01 state15 - 0.584 state37 + 1.13 state47 - 0.667) fires for states 15/47 (-0.2); 26561 -> 8554 chain fires for state 49 (-0.27). Linear fits are exact; AUC contribution of the nonlinearity is nil.
ann_91.proposed: Small shifts for a few states.

ann_92.original: Hypothesis (supported): P(churn) = sigmoid(-3.246 + linear_backbone + csc_low_usage_gate + csc_threshold_low_day + day_minutes_hinge + intl_minutes_hinge + account_length_hinge + vmail_messages_hinge + state_units); all children combine additively in the output logit; the 26 unconnected inputs (totalNightMinutes, totalIntlCharge, all 3 area codes, 21 states) have zero effect. The nonlinear structure is one idea plus one hinge: customer-service calls raise churn risk steeply only when day (and evening) usage is low, and day usage raises risk sharply only in the top quartile. Evidence (train): AUC 0.9081; all children linearised jointly 0.8331 (refit L2 LR 0.8433); restoring the two CSC gates together recovers 0.0693 of the 0.0750 gap, with the day-minutes hinge 0.0745; csc_threshold_low_day alone 0.053, csc_low_usage_gate alone 0.037, day hinge alone 0.031; intl/account/vmail hinges and state units ~0. SHAP (300 rows, probability scale): linear backbone 0.116, 104 0.060, 6238 0.054, 9029 0.025, 7506 0.023, 29980 0.019, others <0.003. Rare categories: state 24 offset -1.60 vs calibrating -0.55; state 42 lifts the day-charge veto on 8 rows; all states off costs 0.0076 AUC.
ann_92.proposed: The predicted chance that a customer leaves rises with an international plan and with daytime minutes, steeply above about 212 minutes; customer-service calls and evening minutes add slightly; higher daytime and evening charges lower it slightly; area code, international charge and night-time minutes are ignored.

summary.text: For a typical customer (in West Virginia, area code 415, with no international or voice-mail plan, one call to customer service and median usage, such as about 180 daytime minutes), having an international plan clearly raises the predicted chance that a customer leaves from about 2% to about 17%.
More daytime minutes (112 to 249) clearly raise it from about 1% to about 14%, and they add to it most once they rise above about 212 (from 0 to 271 minutes, about 2% to 13%).
Being in California instead of West Virginia raises it to about 7% (on the training data only).
More evening minutes (about 1% to 5%) and going from 0 to 3 customer-service calls raise it only slightly.
Higher daytime and evening charges lower it only slightly (on the training data only).
The model ignores area code, total international charge and total night-time minutes.

reference_patient.definition: the typical patient: the median training patient for every number and the most common training category for every category (not a real patient)

confidence_rules.clearly: a meaningful change in predicted risk for a typical patient (at least 5% points), the test split agrees (same sign, and its bootstrap interval over test patients excludes no benefit), and every group has at least 20 training patients
confidence_rules.consistently across patients: the claim holds for at least 90% of training patients (range across patients); this is not a significance statement
confidence_rules.on the training data only: the test split disagrees (opposite sign, or no benefit on test patients) or is unclear (its interval includes no benefit), or no test check is available
confidence_rules.slightly: the change in predicted risk for a typical patient is below 5% points

summary.text: For a typical customer, the model gives a clearly higher predicted chance that a customer leaves if the customer has an international plan (about 17%) than if the customer has no international plan (about 2%).
For a typical customer, total daytime minutes going from 112 minutes to 249 minutes clearly raises the predicted chance that a customer leaves from about 1% to about 14%.

For a typical customer, the model gives a higher predicted chance that a customer leaves if the customer is in California (about 7%) than if the customer is in West Virginia (about 2%) (on the training data only).

Through one part of the model, total daytime minutes only clearly adds to the predicted chance that a customer leaves once it rises above about 212 minutes: for a typical such customer, going from 0 minutes to 271 minutes moves it from about 2% to about 13%.

Through one part of the model, total daytime charge only clearly lowers the predicted chance that a customer leaves while it stays below about 33.06 US dollars for customers in Minnesota: for a typical such customer, going from 15.49 US dollars to 59.76 US dollars moves it from about 10% to about 2%.
The model ignores area code, total international charge and total night-time minutes.
